chapter: Hopkins, Kelly's Stables and Red Allen
title: Claude Hopkins's band: the xylophone collapses
summary: With Claude Hopkins he played rented xylophones and was mistaken for Lionel Hampton, until the instrument collapsed on stage and he gave up vibes after hearing Milt Jackson.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Playing in Lionel Hampton's big band

blocks.x: Well listen, so then Claude heard you and decided he wanted to have that in the band.
Yeah. Yeah. So when I joined Claude I didn't have any vibes, you know.
Because I couldn't use the ones without the damper.

So one day we were in the Howard Theater. This is funny. And for my tune they wheeled out the xylophones in the front of the stage, with the microphone drooping over it and all. So we were playing a tune, I think, 'China Boy,' you know, which I would do this thing, you know, like Lionel Hampton did later, he would do on the piano.
Well, I was doing it then, you know. You know, this was before Lionel came to New York. And everyone thought I was Lionel Hampton.
Because they had never seen Lionel.
Because he was still in California.
I don't think he came with Benny until around '38, '37.
He was with Les Hite Haight.
But we had been hearing about him, but no-one had ever seen him.
So when I came to New York everyone says, 'Are you Lionel?'

So but anyway, to get back to the story, we were in the Howard Theater, and I began to play these xylophones, because I was trying to get -- I could get over them a lot faster than I could the vibes, you know, because the vibes would linger a little bit, you know.
But these xylophones, they were like a piano, you know?

So as I was getting into my chords, and everybody was clapping, yeah, yeah, yeah, you know, and I was playing away, and the whole -- and the xylophones collapsed. They just feel out on the stage. Some screw, you know, by the vibrations, the screw untightened and the whole thing just fell flat on the floor. So Claude Kenny said -- what did he say? Kenny, 'Pick up your bed and walk.'
With that I stopped. That was it. That was it for me. I stopped playing.
That was the end of that?
That was the end of that. Well, you know, I played around but never with a band.
Then when I heard Milt Jackson that convinced me that that wasn't my instrument.
